public_sources.claim_used: Linux flock locks are associated with an open file description rather than a pathname.
rename atomically replaces the destination pathname while already-open file descriptors for the old pathname remain unaffected.

result: The previously validated data-file-flock writer has a same-host pathname-replacement hole that same-inode append races do not exercise. The exact current writer source was byte-reconstructed and Git-blob verified as 70843c8011eed717001d31cfe59028beb86739c4. Two deterministic multiprocessing reproductions succeeded: (1) replacement of the pathname while an old-inode writer held flock allowed a second exact writer to lock and append the replacement inode concurrently; (2) more strongly, a cooperative repair that itself flocked the data file could replace the pathname after another writer had opened but before that writer acquired flock, after which the preopened writer locked/appended the now-unlinked old inode while a new writer appended the replacement inode. Both writers reported exact readback success, but only the replacement-inode append remained visible at the pathname. A candidate stable-sidecar lock acquired before opening/replacing the data path eliminated the tested race: 500 randomized append-vs-repair races and 500 duplicate-append races had zero double-success/final-state violations.
validated_contracts: The current PosixFlockedCASAppendWriter source used by the reproduction exactly matched Git blob 70843c8011eed717001d31cfe59028beb86739c4.

Data-file flock does not serialize operations across pathname replacement because the lock is tied to the open file description/inode while rename can redirect the pathname to a different inode without invalidating existing descriptors.

The open-before-lock ordering creates a cooperative TOCTOU surface: a writer may open inode A, a repair may lock A and atomically replace the pathname with inode B, then the first writer may later lock and append A while another writer locks/appends B.

Under the tested single-host cooperative protocol, acquiring one stable non-replaced sidecar lock before opening or replacing the journal pathname serialized both append and repair. In 500 randomized append-vs-repair races exactly one operation won each round; in 500 duplicate-append races exactly one append won each round.
Directory fsync after repair rename is required by the candidate repair path for rename durability; the stable lock must remain held through replacement and exact readback.
measurement_validity_rules: Same-inode writer races are insufficient evidence for pathname-based journal serialization when crash repair may truncate by rename/replacement. Concurrency validation must include inode replacement and open-before-lock interleavings.
A pathname-level CAS plus flock on the data file is not a stable fencing primitive if the pathname can be rebound to a new inode while another process has the old inode open.

For single-host cooperative repair, use a protocol-stable lock inode acquired before any data-file open/replace, and require every append and repair path to share it. Never rename/unlink/replace the lock inode itself.

Successful fsync/readback on an open descriptor proves durability for that descriptor's inode, not that the pathname still names that inode. Scientific durability checks must include pathname identity/serialization across repair.
Do not generalize this sidecar lock to distributed storage; multi-host execution requires storage-enforced monotonic fencing or another distributed serialization primitive.
scope_limitations: The race was reproduced on the local Linux filesystem/runtime available in this execution. It establishes an existence counterexample for the current single-host data-file-flock design, not a frequency estimate for production deployments.

The stable-sidecar validation covers cooperative local processes that all use the same sidecar lock and a filesystem where POSIX flock is reliable. It does not cover NFS, object stores, multi-host writers, malicious/uncooperative bypass, or replacement/unlink of the sidecar lock itself.

The test targets writer/repair serialization. It did not yet run the full ADMIT/RESERVE/SLOT/COMMIT/CLOSE provenance runtime concurrently with repair, so scientific event-level one-launch/one-reservation guarantees remain to be revalidated after writer substitution.
No claim extends beyond the exact tested race, stable-lock candidate, and stated filesystem/process assumptions.
frontier: Substitute the stable-sidecar writer into both main-journal and reservation-ledger append paths and make torn-tail truncate/replace recovery acquire the same stable lock before inspecting or replacing the data pathname.

Run one multiprocessing lifecycle that races duplicate ADMIT, duplicate RESERVE, late SLOT versus deadline CLOSE, and torn-tail repair/replacement while using the stable-sidecar writer; require one durable reservation, one scorer launch, no stale-path success, and exact final compliance replay.

Add a mechanical invariant that the sidecar lock pathname/inode is protocol-stable and never repaired by rename; test process death while holding the sidecar flock and restart recovery from a torn data tail.

If deployment can span hosts or storage without reliable flock, replace the local sidecar scheme with a monotonic fencing-token store that rejects stale fence values; do not infer distributed safety from this result.
exact_next_action: Build a stable-lock-aware repair facade that acquires the same sidecar lock before decode/truncate-or-replace and expose it as the only allowed repair path. Then inject StableSidecarFlockedCASWriter into the existing provenance runtime and run the combined multiprocessing lifecycle: duplicate ADMITs, duplicate RESERVEs, one scorer-attempt race, SLOT/COMMIT versus deadline CLOSE, and a concurrent torn-tail repair. Reject any execution where a writer reports success on an inode no longer named by the journal path or where final compliance replay differs across restart.
